opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that paper is really interesting, and I think it's measuring something real, but I'd push back on the conclusion people draw from it.

What they showed is that if you take the base model and sample it enough times, say pass@256 or pass@1000, the base model's coverage of correct answers is comparable to, or sometimes even exceeds, the RL'd model's. And the RL'd model is much better at pass@1. So the story people tell is that RL just sharpens the distribution. It takes reasoning paths the base model already had somewhere in its tail and makes them the default, rather than teaching anything fundamentally new.

I think that's a reasonable description of what's happening at current RL compute scales, and I want to stress that qualifier. The amount of compute going into RL right now is still tiny compared to pretraining. If you put a small amount of optimization pressure on a model, of course you're mostly reweighting what's already there. That's what a small amount of optimization pressure does. The question is what happens when you scale it up, and I don't think that paper can tell you that.

There's also a point about what pass@k at very large k actually means. If you sample a thousand times and one sample is right, has the model "got" that capability? On a math problem with a verifiable answer, a model producing a thousand varied attempts can stumble onto the right one in a way that's a bit like monkeys at typewriters, at least partially. Being able to reliably find the answer, to know which path to commit to and chain many steps without derailing, is the capability that matters. Turning a one-in-a-thousand success into a nine-in-ten success isn't nothing. In some sense that's the whole game.

The bigger point is that on long-horizon tasks, eliciting and creating start to blur. If you can reliably do step one, then step two, then step three, and each was only latent before, then a thousand-step task that the base model would essentially never complete becomes possible. Its probability under the base model is effectively zero even if every individual step was "in there." So I'd say RL is doing more than surfacing pre-existing capabilities. It's composing them, and composition at length looks a lot like a new capability.

And we have existence proofs from the past. AlphaGo and AlphaZero clearly discovered things that weren't in human play. Move 37 wasn't in the prior. Given a clean enough reward signal and enough compute, RL finds genuinely new knowledge. The constraint for language models has been the quality of the reward signal and how much compute we've been willing to spend, not some fundamental limit of the method.

So my summary is that the paper is a good snapshot of RL at small scale on fairly short tasks, and I'd expect that picture to change as RL compute grows and tasks get longer and more agentic.

r001.rationale: The response says current RL compute is tiny compared with pretraining and frames the paper as a snapshot of RL at small scale.

r002.rationale: It links small optimization compute to mostly reweighting existing capabilities and says scaling compute could change what RL teaches.

r003.rationale: It cites AlphaGo and AlphaZero’s discoveries as evidence that clean reward signals and enough compute can produce genuinely new knowledge.

r004.rationale: It says the constraint is reward quality and compute, rather than a fundamental limit of the method.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think that paper is doing something quite careful and interesting, but I think the conclusion people drew from it is a lot stronger than what the experiment actually shows.

Let me steelman it first. What they found is that if you take the base model and sample, say, 256 times on a math problem, the pass-at-k curve of the base model eventually catches up to and even crosses the RL'd model. So the reasoning model is better at pass-at-one, but the base model has the same "coverage" of correct answers if you're willing to try enough times. And from that they infer that RL isn't teaching the model anything new, it's just sharpening the distribution toward answers that were already in there.

A few things I'd push on.

The first is that pass-at-k with a verifier is not a capability in any practically useful sense. If I give you a model that gets the answer right one time in 256 and you need an oracle to tell you which one, you don't have a model that can do math. You have a random generator plus a grader. The entire value of RL here is collapsing that into something that gets it right the first time, reliably, without the oracle. Calling that "merely eliciting" undersells what's happening. The thing we actually care about is the pass-at-one behavior, because that's what compounds when you chain steps together in a long task.

The second is that the setup was pretty narrow. They were looking at relatively small models, a relatively small amount of RL compute, on a domain like competition math where the base model has already seen an enormous amount of relevant data. Of course the correct answers are in the support of the distribution for AIME-style problems. The question is what happens when you're far enough into training that the model is doing things that don't exist anywhere in pretraining, where the base model's pass-at-k curve stays flat no matter how long you sample. And I'd also say the amount of RL compute in that study is a tiny fraction of what the frontier labs are putting in. The shape of these curves at a thousand RL steps and the shape at a hundred thousand are not the same.

The third thing, and this is the one I feel most strongly about, is that the distinction between "eliciting" and "creating" gets blurry when you think about what capability is. Every capability a model learns is, in some sense, in the space of programs its weights could represent. Pretraining elicits things too. The interesting question isn't whether the answer existed somewhere in the distribution, it's whether the model can find it, and at what cost. If RL moves something from one-in-a-thousand to nine-in-ten, and you chain fifty of those steps together in an agentic task, you've gone from a system that essentially never completes the task to one that does it routinely. That's not a cosmetic change.

Now, where I do think they're pointing at something real: in the early phase of RL, a lot of what's happening probably is distribution sharpening. The model already has the right ideas and is just learning to commit to them. And there's a genuine open question about how much of the gain comes from that versus genuinely new reasoning strategies. I'd love to see that work extended with much more compute and in domains where the base model is at zero. My bet, from what we see internally, is that the picture looks quite different there. But that's an empirical claim, and the right response to the paper is to run that experiment, not to decide the question in advance either way.

r001.rationale: The response says the study used a tiny fraction of the RL compute frontier labs use, but does not compare the study’s RL compute with its base-model training compute.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute amounts but does not present training compute as a proxy for how much new knowledge or capability training adds.

r003.rationale: The response does not cite superhuman game-playing performance or clean reinforcement signals as evidence that RL can teach new knowledge.

r004.rationale: It says capabilities can be viewed as programs the weights could represent, but does not assert that RL has no structural limitation on adding new knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s evidence for a narrower claim than “reinforcement learning only elicits existing capabilities.” If the base model can solve a problem given enough attempts, then yes, the successful answer was already somewhere in its distribution. But that doesn’t tell you how useful the model is, or what reinforcement learning can ultimately teach it.

Imagine one model solves a problem once in a million attempts and another solves it half the time. There’s a sense in which they both “had the capability,” but that definition is missing most of what we care about. Especially if you don’t have a cheap way to identify which of those million answers is correct.

The more interesting question is whether reinforcement learning is just increasing the probability of particular solutions the model could already produce, or learning strategies that generalize to new problems. Matching performance with enough samples doesn’t distinguish those explanations. You’d want to look at how the models perform on unfamiliar problems, with comparable compute budgets, and how that changes as you scale training.

So I’d take the result seriously as evidence that base models have more latent reasoning ability than a single attempt reveals. I wouldn’t take it as establishing a ceiling on what reinforcement learning can do.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the compute used for reinforcement learning with the compute used to train the base model.

r002.rationale: It does not describe training compute as a proxy for added knowledge or capability.

r003.rationale: It does not cite superhuman game-playing as evidence about what clean reinforcement signals can teach.

r004.rationale: It questions whether the study establishes a ceiling, but does not assert that reinforcement learning has no structural barrier to adding new knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish “the model has some probability of producing the right answer” from “the model can reliably solve the problem.” Those are very different things. If you give a base model enough attempts, you can find some very impressive outputs. But you also need a way of identifying which attempt is correct, and that can be as hard as solving the original problem.

So I think that result is interesting, but the word “only” is doing a lot of work in “RL only elicits existing capabilities.” Turning something that happens once in a thousand attempts into something that happens most of the time is a substantial improvement in capability. And changing which intermediate steps the model takes changes which problems it can reach solutions to within a fixed compute budget.

There’s also a distinction between what a particular experiment demonstrates and what reinforcement learning can do in principle. You might find that an initial round of RL mostly concentrates probability on successful trajectories that the base model already samples. That doesn’t establish that further training can’t discover new strategies. Successful behaviors become more common, and then they become the starting point for further exploration.

The comparison I’d want is performance at matched inference compute, with the cost of selecting an answer included, and then how that changes as you scale training. Matching performance with enough attempts is evidence about the base model’s distribution. It isn’t, by itself, a ceiling on what RL can achieve.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the study’s reinforcement-learning compute with base-model training compute.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling training but does not identify training compute as a proxy for how much new knowledge or capability training adds.

r003.rationale: It does not cite superhuman game-playing as evidence that clean reinforcement signals can teach new knowledge.

r004.rationale: The response says further training might discover new strategies, but does not assert that neural networks have no structural limitation on gaining new knowledge through reinforcement learning.
